title: Steel Division: Normandy 44
text: My quick thoughts thus far, after just a couple skirmishes: #1 - The balance still needs work. Right now, the most problematic balance issue is the recon and sight range of non-recon units. Armored units right now feel extraordinarily vulnerable, and the reason is the ridiculously poor sight-range they have. I totally understand if my armor doesn't see enemy units that are stationary in a forest nearby and take a close-range AT weapon hit and go up in flames. What is harder to understand is when an enemy infantry unit is moving in open ground right a little ways away, yet manages to still take the tank out because they weren't seen until the tank was on top of them *in an open field, while the enemy was moving*. #2 - Anti-air vs Anti-tank efficiency is insane. AT weapons can frequently 1 or 2 shot a tank... anti-air seemed to never make a single kill against air units (though they do have some power against infantry and ground targets). It seems wildly inconsistent that anti-tank units do pretty well, while my only prayer of actually destroying enemy aircraft is with my own. I mean, come on: I have 88-mm AA guns spread around the area I know the enemy aircraft will enter, and they enter only to be nothing more than scared off. I get that my own aircraft should be better at destroying enemy air-power, but if I have multiple AA guns firing on a target, I should have more than a 5% chance to shoot it down. #3 - I'm not sure I'm a fan of the phase system. It's pretty arbitrary, even in terms of game mechanics and balance... previous games Eugen made basically used the income economics to regulate when you got a chance to get out particular units, which was more flexible and allowed players to rush out an expensive unit quite early at the risk of not having the support units to back it up. This time around, the phase system arbitrarily keeps units out of the game until X amount of time passes. #4 - I like the dynamic battlelines element. It means that map control can be approached very fluidly and flexibly. Rather than have some static point to capture, the entire map itself is worth something, netting extra income to players that find ways to break the enemy line and squeeze a few units through. #5 - CPU play is solid, and probably a step up from the already decent play of the Wargame series' CPU. The only thing I've seen thus far that is problematic is that the CPU sure likes to bunch up its units, allowing human players to really get a lot out of their artillery and bombers. Overall, it's fun. A bit more micro-intensive than Total War games, a little harder to know what is and isn't in cover compared to CoH2, but a lot more action-packed than the typical Paradox games (I love EU-IV and Stellaris, but exercises in intense planning and weighing of risk/reward sometimes needs to give way to a couple hours of actually controlling the combat and watching stuff blow up).

title: Steel Division: Normandy 44
text: You’ll be ordering troops, tanks, artillery and other assorted machines of bloody warfare around the lovingly rendered maps of Normandy in a bid to win. Unlike other RTS games you won’t be building bases or any other structures. Instead, you’ll have an initial amount of points to spend on deploying your first batch of troops and armor onto your portion of the map. Here you also have a chance to give them their starting orders before the match starts, examining the map for points you’d like to assault straight away or perhaps even setting up a full-blown rush for enemy territory. Once you hit the launch button you’ll begin acquiring more requisition points every minute, and the number of these depends entirely on the division you’re playing as. With these you can bring new units onto the field, although they’ll always enter from your starting area so if you’ve captured a huge chunk of the map it can take some time for reinforcements to trundle across the road network to your position. As the battle progresses you’ll move through three phases, with new units becoming available in each phase. Sometimes these will simply be more powerful and expensive troops, tanks and weapons, but other times it may simply be MORE of the same units since you have a limited amount of each to chuck into the fight. The most difficult part of the entire game can be understanding the subtle differences between the staggering 400 units available to you across all of the various divisions. The user interface is generally pretty good, but when you begin staring at the various stats it’s easy to feel like you’ve stepped into a maths lesson half way through and have no idea what the hell is going on. caters to a particular audience of hardcore strategy fans,  but this difficult to master game won’t be for everyone. - Fantastic level of detail and historical accuracy - Clever use of extensive Battlegroup system - Realism has a positive effect on gameplay - Steep learning curve - Imbalances with certain unit types - Much micro-management DISASTER | BAD | MEDIOCRE | OKAY | GOOD | | AMAZING | MASTERPIECE

title: Stellar Tactics
text: I bought this game last night, it was cheaper than my takeaway.  I ate the takeaway whilst it downloaded.  I have only three hours on record as I write this - I cleared the first section, that I might call the prologue, or tutorial, (It's not just a tutorial it's real content) - and I had just gotten into the next part of the game.  To say I'm excited is an understatement.  Maybe it's just the right match for my peculiar tastes or whatever, I don't know, but I enjoyed very much the first introductory, prologue like, tutorial-like bit of the game.  I'm really not paying much interest in work today and am just trying to get as much info from the dev twitter, this forum, etc.  A game's not captured my imagination and enthusiasm like this for a long while. The game put me in mind of a whole load of games I've previously enjoyed.  The game obviously benefits from the creator's distinct style, which is consistent and believable.  I had no issues with any suspension of disbelief and was totally engrossed, well past the time I should have gone to bed.  Games that, stylistically, it reminds me of are things like Cybermercs, System Shock, Alien Swarm, etc.  It is a solid turn-based team tactics game.  It's got Fallout Tactics, Jagged Alliance, XCOm, etc.  That's all in there.  It has an old school RPG stats and skills character sheet.  It's got lots of loot.  It's got equipment slots and stats on the equipment for character stat boosts, so there is stuff for people who like putting builds together.  I found the weapon's nicely different, the weapon classes that is.  The art work and the sound are consistent, the sound design is very good actually.  I was just thinking about the pictures of the weapons and the audio, and that consistent cyber-punk style is present.  It's also got melee going on - and that's handled better than I expected. Alone; the above would have me like the game.  After all, that is as much as I've played so far.  But I'm given to understand that this is also a procedurally generated place.  The story actually seems good, I already care about the main NPC character, I already have feelings about the initial villain character.  That aspect alone and the dialogue make my think fondly of the Shadow Run games, and other commenters have made that connection too.  But the potential to take my squad into randomly generated, non-story, content has me really excited.  To make my own narrative, on top of the author's story, I find really appealing.  I miss a sense of exploration in a lot of titles, and it is great that the game describes being able to visit space stations, caves, old ruins, etc.  I'm looking forward to exploring.  It is like an up-to-date MegaTraveller, but with random content and procedural generation.  It has a lot of the MegaTraveller feel!! Being able to explore has me super excited, as you can probably tell.  What I'm also extremely excited about is the other side to the game.  Where you fly your space ship cruiser around.  A different game part.  Like the difference between the strategic game and the tactical game in a Total War type game.  The ability to fly somewhere, find something interesting, and then walk around it is something you don't often get.  Sid Meyer's Pirates sort of did it, but there wasn't much tactical content other than the fight once you got to port.  I suppose the XCOM analogy comes back again here - but without the reactionary nature of the alien sites.  The idea of just finding stuff and then the player having a choice to just explore, or move on, is ace.  An ancient game called Exile always stayed with me, because you could go into your spaceship which was landed on the planet - it felt like home.  I can imagine, if I'd been playing this game and things had gone badly on a random mission and I run away, being back on the ship will feel safe.  I can see I will find just that subtle thing immensely immersive. There's going to be space combat too, if it isn't already in.  From the demo graphics it looks like a cross between EVE Online and Space Wolves or something similar.  That will be ace. So - I've not touched the space ships bit, and I've not started doing my random exploration yet.  But what's there already is superb.  I'm very excited about this.  It ticks so many boxes for me, I'm sure it will for other people as well.

title: Stellar Tactics
text: Stellar Tactics: ~~~~~~~~~~~ The “Phase virus” is bringing mankind to its knees! But that was not the worst of it; a meteor homing for earth was the last straw.  The fight for survival was intense and the best of humankind (not infected) worked day and night to build four massive spaceships to send the remaining healthy humans to space to find new worlds to colonize. BEEP. BEEP. BEEP . . .  you’re just being woken up! BEEP.BEEP.BEEP. . . You and your team are on one of these spaceships! Welcome to Stellar Tactics! Stellar Tactics is an adventure / action / turned-based combat game set in a space environment. First, it’s customization time! Yes, you will have to create your four men’s or women’s (mixed if you like) squad. You will be able to mix and match faces, hair, complexity and voices for each of your characters - plenty of fun there. Add some points to your attributes (strength, dexterity, agility and more) as well as your skills in weaponry, hand-to-hand combat and specialities (hacking, crafting and others). When you are done, your four-person squad will be awoken from their deep sleep capsules.  You will be greeted by Dr Rhamus, a top scientist on board your spaceship. You quickly find out that your squad is a special elite force and the reason for your sudden wake-up call is that the “Phage Virus” contaminated personnel on your giant spacecraft. The “Phague Virus” attaches itself to the neurological system and destroys the brain host; in short, you become a zombie if you are affected! Upon this great introduction, you will be sent to accomplish quests. As you go through the spaceship, your squad will be able to search boxes, cabinets, wardrobes for items (ammunition, money and other things). It will be very easy to spot by using the LCTRL key. As soon as your squad encounters one or more enemies, the turn-based combat will automatically take over. I hope you have found enough ammunition, because you will need it! Each of you characters will have movement and action points. So, the trick is to be able to see your foe and be able to target and shoot them. Long-range weapons will help you shoot from a distance and depending on what you are using, you can set up your gun to shoot just one or a burst of bullets. The enemies are fast and not easy to defeat, to be honest with you. Some will fight bare-handed but others will shoot projectiles from their hands, or even use metal objects to inflict personal injury. During the battle, one or several of your personel might obtain skill upgrades or even level up. If that’s the case, make sure to open your character page and distribute points to your characters attributes. Very nice graphics with a good story so far. The commands need to be much smoother in my opinion, sometimes it can take a couple of clicks to get your squad to move, which can be annoying. A mini map would be helpful too. Positives: ~~~~~~~ -	Good graphics -	Interesting story -	Great character customization -	Good turn-based combat Negatives: ~~~~~~~~ -	Controls need to be smoother -	No achievements or trading cards (at this stage) This is a very impressive early access game – I am glad to have Stellar Tactics in my game library. 8/10 Key provided by developer/publisher for review purposes. Any opinions expressed are entirely my own!

title: Stellar Tactics
text: Really, really, REALLY slow paced.  Character movement is slow, plot progression is slow, even the bullets are slow! Maybe I'll return and give it another chance someday, but for now, it's just another indie game gathering dust in my collection.

title: Stellar Tactics
text: Firstly; This is not your usual EA lucky-bag app.  This game is a large ambitious project. So what do you have? You have turn based tactical combat, fully animated with true LOS.  You also have the neat ability to fine-tune your attacks, hold down 'alt' and pick the body part you want to shoot/hit. You have a more than competent character generator, portrait, skills, traits, etc: You have free roam space exploration.  Yep! you fly a space ship in a massive seed based universe. Your characters take up stations on said spaceship. Story is cliche but well told. The developer seems to be dedicated and very skilled.  The speed in which he works is quite amazing, not to mention his decision to change engine mid production.  I have known other dev's faced with engine change abandon the present project and move on to their next, but this developer doesn't seem to mess about, he get's the job done.  You have to respect that. The game is fun to play even at this early stage, and the vision of what it's to become would make the final game, fantastic, no doubt on that score. Is this game worth your support?  Yes, very much so. *Review will be updated as development progresses.

title: Stellaris
text: This game is fantastic! It has all the intricate elements that I've been looking for in a space 4x game, and the real time pause/play feature seems much better than turn based games like this! The races are sooo extensive and unique, custom build one to see for yourself! I made my first race and I am loving it thus far. Please, check out this game if you haven't already. I am absolutely loving it! I will keep my review up to date as I continue playing. I should also not that I play lots of games like this: gal civ 3, sid meier's civ 5, total war games etc. This one is different... Stellaris features multiple things that set it apart from its competitors: 1) Pause/play global action. All fights, events, exploration... everything in the game is real time pause/play! (no turns) 2) Unique research method of generating 3 options at a time (no tree). 3) Control not just one leader, but multiple leaders that serve under your main one(s). 4) Expand planetary building functionality as your population steadily expands across the planets. 5) The MOST EXTENSIVE character/faction creation system in this kind of game yet. 6) Unique art style, featuring ANIMATED 2-D character icons that work extremely well for the variety of races. 7) SOOOOOO many races! (With more surely to follow) 8) Unique planet types with habitation possible even in extreme conditions. 9) Unique alert system that compliments the pause/play global function well. 10) Extensive star systems and unique means of traveling between said systems. 11) Events that make mention of YOUR unique empire name (event mission chains of sorts). 12) Speed up and slow down time globally as you please. Want that research done now? High speed baby!!! I am certain that there are more amazing things that I am either forgetting at the moment or have yet to encounter, but I am loving this game thus far. It is worth every penny that I spent on it, and I got the most expensive version! I can't wait to see what they have in store for the future DLC and steam workshop content that modders will add! I am also looking forward to checking out the art book and novel that were included with my purchase. Verdict: 10/10 (will continue updating) p.s. My only complaint isn't even really a valid complaint. I ordered the most expensive edition (forget what it was called) and was kindof hoping to receive physical copies of the novel, signed poster and perhaps the artbook. All of it was digital though. It is fine, I am enjoying that extra content. For some weird reason I thought it may ship to my house but I guess I was wrong.

title: Stellaris
text: Recommended. The new, updated version of the old classics like Master of Orion, Space Empires and Galactic Civilizations, but instead of turn-based this game is real-time with the option to pause. Way off from the earlier games of Paradox, this still is a very solid game, especially if you like these kind of space-civ building games. Very nice touches are the ability to completely customize your race, but also to allow custom made races to be drawn into future games as AI opponents. Also, Paradox events are part of this game, so expect a few laughters while reading through event descriptions, and there's more than a few references to historical events that could've taken place here on earth. Still, compared to other similar games, this feels slightly streamlined, but I suppose that's on par with Paradox products. If you consider EU, CK or some other of their titles, much detail never went into the tactical parts, how machines were to be made or what composition units would have except for a variation of base troop types. In that sense, having 4 types of base ships that can be modified somewhat according to your liking is decent enough I suppose, but this and the sort of slim options on planet building, coupled with the almost total absence of tactics is the drawbacks of this title. They don't bug me much though, those shortcomings I just listed. This game really shines in its strategic parts, and diplomacy can be really interesting and unexpected. There's options for building federations, as well as having vassals, contributaries and so forth, to alliances, non-agression pacts, trade deals and different types of war. The difference in war is determined by your nations focus, as pacifists wont' be able to wage conquest wars for example. As for the strategic parts, instead of going for one of the classic star-travel choices of warp, wormhole or starlane hyperdrive, this game has all three. You'll get to choose one, and strategy will differ depending on what you pick. The game also contains alot of references to sci-fi movies, like the alien genetic xeno-troopers, that turns out as "Bio-warfare divisions" and contains Xenomorphs (I guess finally got their way, huh?), so it's clear that the homework has been done on sci-fi as well, wich at least helps me appreciate a game like this even more, and you can be the sci-fi component as well, by invading planets that have sentient beings that hasn't reached space yet. Land your troops amongst atomic-age sentient mammal beings, or establish an observation post in orbit, silently observing, try to enlighten them with technology, or maybe stay hidden and just do secret experiments on them, the choice is all yours. Finally, there's also domestic politics, with different fractions, unrest, potential revolts and whatever you could imagine, and if you have aliens to your race as slaves in your area, expect an emancipation movement to start sooner or later. You can make political decisions, and those decisions will have an impact, not only on what your empire can do in the galaxy, but will also impact home opinion, and as always, there's always some people happy about a certain direction, as there's always people unhappy about it. All in all, this makes for a game with surprising depth, and not all you can do have been mentioned in this review. As such it's well worth picking up and can provide with lots and lots of good gaming time. Some parts could've been more complex, but I suppose it's a balance between it all. One thing is for sure though, and that is that it is solid as it stands, and have potential to become a true classic. My opinion on Paradox DLCs are that they're very often solid and mostly brings new, interesting and depthening concepts to their games, so it's anyones guess how good this could actually end up becoming.

text: I've been interested in Stellaris for a long time and held off buying it based on others' reviews, but I can safely report that I believe it is worth the money.  Everyone's expectations are different, but I feel it strikes that 4X itch while still being varied and exciting enough to make me want to play again and again.  I'm more of a hardcore Civ V player than Europa Universalis, and I'm very pleased with the game.  RECOMMENDED! PROS + Empire, policies, races, civics, beliefs...everything customizable + Early exploration is exciting + Lots of different types of civilizations to interact with + AI feels intelligent (allies frequently sent me supportive units in war) + Excellent sense of progression and flow from beginning to end + Lots of quests and events keeps things interesting + Realistic sector system automates a lot of micromanagement CONS - Long periods of peace can get boring - Paid DLC feels like it should be included in base game - High learning curve - Earning achievements requires Iron Man Mode (Hardcore, no Save)

title: Stellaris
text: Excellent game with a few rough edges that the modding community are busy sorting out.  If you are new to Paradox games then prepare yourself for a learning curve that, while not as steep by any means as the likes of Eu4, isn't a simple bump in the road.  You will need some patience, especially in the mid game when things appear to slow to a crawl.  Be assured however that there is a crap ton of stuff going on under the hood and you will eventually learn to identify and deal with it.  The depth of Stellaris is unmatched and there are little stories going on all over the place as well as the big picture. A new race to the stars popped up nearby having got themselves off terrafirma and were pretty terrified of it all, especially as their first contact was a powerful empire of space arachnids.  Through diplomacy they found that actually the spiders were not that bad.  I offered them protectorate status and they eagerly accepted.  Shortly after a beligerent empire came along and attacked them, obviously not realising the consequences, which they soon learned as their homeworld came face to face with a spider invasion.  They are now my vassels.  They don't like it but that's just tough for them because I don't like bullies who hit my little friends. I am over 130 hours into the game so I have had my monies worth and then some.  Unfortunately the game is struggling to come up with an answer as to what it wants to be.  During development I raised a concern that attempting to create a hybrid between grand strategy and 4x was, in my opinion, foolish as Paradox were trying to appeal to two distinctly different types of gamers and it turns out that I was right, although I take no pleasure in it.  With the recent Clarke patch the game has lurched more towards 4x in the early stages and it was heavy 4x early on to start with.  People complained about the Ai being too passive so Paradox, in typical developer fashion, have rammed the lever too far in the opposite direction.  Now you can end up with a scenario ( which I had in a recent game ) where an empire will declare all out war on you simply because it can.  Now, that would be fine for xenophobic empires as it would be like an arachnaphobic striking out violently against the spider that got too close, but the empire that declared war on me for no good reason were not even close to being xenophobic, and in fact had an oppinion of me of +72.  I beat them after a shortish war and 16 years later they were at it again. My point here is that the old 4x meme of 'I'm bigger than you so I want your stuff' has almost become front and centre.  At release Stellaris felt like an early paradox game but if Clarke is anything to go by the grand strategy players may as well throw the game onto the dusty shelf while the 4x players enjoy the experience until mid game when it slows to a crawl and fails completely to take them with it on it's faltering journey into the non-existant diplomacy of what should be a deep and interesting experience, and misses the mark by a wide margin. Certainly Clarke made some improvments to various systems like sector Ai but most of those improvments were in response to the loud voices of the 4x players that were unsatisfied with the game.  The second patch 'Asimov' has a lot to do and will be make or break for Stellaris.  If it doesn't redress the balance then the traditional Paradox gamer will simply head on over to HOI4 or back to Eu4 while the game tries to keep it's new 4x players ( not gonna happen ) with a number of other promising 4x titles just over the next hill poised ready to take it's crown. As it stands I will still give the game a thumbs up but that will change if Asimov doesn't deliver the goods.  Mixing genres rarely ends well and Stellaris is on the brink.

title: Still Life
text: Still Life follows the trail of a gruesome serial killer in a classic thriller/mystery style. You play as detective Victoria McPherson who is investigating a string of prosti tute murders, all of whom's bodies were found badly beaten and mutilated. The atmosphere is well done and each crime scene is quite graphic. The style of this game is a classic point and click adventure. As far as game play is concerned, adventure games tend to be vague and it can be difficult to figure out what you are supposed to do next, but that rarely happens in this title. In fact, in Still Life, it is usually very obvious what you are supposed to do - but that's the hard part. The puzzles in this game range from rather simple to frustratingly demanding. While the puzzles do become immensely complex, the puzzles are also very logical. I personally spent about 30-40 minutes trying to figure out one of the difficult puzzles in this game. So if you are going to play this title, you need to have patience and a strong penchant for puzzle solving. This isn't a title you can just rush through (unless you look up all the solutions, but that seems kind of silly). The graphics are a bit dated and the voice acting while good/ok, isn't top notch. About 8-10 hours playtime. 7.5/10 Please upvote this review if you found it useful :)

title: Still Life
text: Still Life is a sequal to the Post Mortem set 80 years later focusing on Vic McPherson, granddaughter of Gus McPherson. A young female agent working for the FBI in Chicago who stumbles upon a series of murders that are all connected to a case Gus was involved with 80 years prior. Unlike the Post Mortem game, this entry of the "Still Life" trilogy is done differently. There's no series of multiple dialoge choices so it's a more linear storyline and the cast of characters are what make this game a real joy to play. I did enjoy the characters from Post Mortem, but the cast of Still Life takes the prize on that category. Vic is a cool heroine full of attitude, humor, and spunk. She's the type of woman I would ask out on a date. While the background designs are much more elabrate and the music score is very top notch than what was present in Post Mortem. The Chicago masked killer is more memorible than the Paris masked killer with the whole motif of Jack the Ripper meets the Phantom of the Opera. Overall the game is a living form of art that will please the eye of art lovers or video game designers.

While it doesn't have the action element of battles or platforming skills required to progress, at no point throughout my playthrough did I feel like I wasn't playing a game.  In fact, adding in some mechanic to impede exploration (difficult jumps, monsters, etc) would actually have detracted from the game and made it much less enjoyable.  Playing really feels like being on an adventure, an adventure of curiosity.  I would love to see more games made like this one.

text: Submerged is comparable to Brothers: A Tale of Two Sons, in that there is no dialogue that is in english, no combat, and a compelling story. title: Submerged
text: Submerged is a game that is solely about exploration.  It's vast yet empty world creates a haunted landscape filled with secrets and collectibles for you to acquire.  The graphics in this game are stunning, and more then that, the world itself is imaginatively  put together.  The sunken city seems to combine elements from a variety of cultures leaving you wondering both where and what was this city.  What happened here?  What happened to the world?  And the answers can be found through a few hours of thorough combing through the cities buildings and many landmarks.  As day turns to night and night to day you will constantly find yourself stopping to take a moment to appreciate how the light is hitting the water, how the animals seem to move keeping the world alive, yet still barren.  The music creates a perfect ambiance to back this journey of exploration. The only area where this game really seems to lag is in the gameplay.  The actual gameplay elements are all perfectly functional, but far too simplistic.  I found myself growing tired of the climbing within the first few buildings because there was just no challenge.  There's two parts to gamplay, riding in your boat and climbing.  The climbing is just pointing the direction you want to go and nothing else.  And the gameplay never evolves.  The only thing that changes throughout the 2 hours it will take you to complete the basic storyline is the boost on your boat increases as you collect other fallen boats.  I would have loved a more challenging climbing system, or possibly some obstacles to overcome/puzzles to solve, something to add a bit difficulty.  Without is the game can seem to start dragging at times. Overall through I would say in all elements except for gameplay this game was a 10/10 for me.  Gameplay is a 6/10 -perfectly functional but lacks engagement or escalation.  I would absolutely recommend this to anyone who might be looking for a game a bit more cathartic, or relaxing, or who just really wants to see what a strong imaginative team of developers can come up with when they really try to create something beautiful.

title: Submerged
text: I'll start by saying I enjoyed it and for the $2 I payed for it the game is nice. However, I'd never pay $20. I can only recommend getting it during a huge sale. Graphics The graphics are nice enough, but unpolished. They remind me of early PS3 fare. There's a lot of weird clipping that goes on but there's nothing game-breaking. Atmosphere This is the purpose of the game and I think it pulls it off well. I quickly got the sense of the environment and backdrop which actually let me guess the story without more than a couple "secrets". It's eerie and calming at the same time. Gameplay Repetitive but calming, so it fits in the game's overall theme. Gameplay consists of boating and climbing up/down ledges and pipes. That's pretty much it. Story Nearly non-existent but there's definitely enough there to intrigue me. Unfortunately the game sets up a world with an intriguing past, an interesting present and a tenuous future then does nothing with it. Your actions are ultimately insignificant and rather pointless in the grand scheme of things. This along with the tiny playtime are the huge negatives for me. Game Length Tiny. 2 hours is what it took for me to unlock half the achievements, beat the game and find over half of the secrets. If you wanted to you could easily beat the game and still be able to refund it. So again, it's worth it if you want a sedate, short exploration game. Just get it on a big sale.

title: Submerged
text: Submerged is rather short but visually engaging little post-apocalyptic climbing-adventure game. Graphics 7.5 of 10 I have mixed feelings about the graphics. Sometimes it's outright stunning with beautiful sunsets on the ruins of a lost civilization and at other times it reminds me of the last gen consoles , or even worse. Music 7 of 10 I liked the music, still I have a feeling it could have been better. There is almost no voice-acting, but sometimes the two kids talk in their strange language, which has no real explanation. But it's rather self explaining. Gameplay 7.5 of 10 You play the little girl and you have to climb and explore the various ruins of old skyscrapers. Which is basically the whole gameplay.If you like to explore a little you'll also able to find fragments of the old world and little hints what happened to the family and the civilization.  No you won't find a rocket launcher here or hordes of zombies. In fact there is zero fighting in this game. So if you're into that stuff, this game is not for you. Story 7.5 of 10 You play the little unnamed girl and your goal is to find medicine, bandages and food for your injured brother. The story is very basic and not very complex , but it's sweet nonetheless. Final verdict I recommend this game to anyone who likes a beautiful atmosphere and doesn't mind the shortness and the lack of combat.
